'''Evelyn Prescott Wiggin''' (1900–1964) was an American [[mathematician]] and university professor. She was one of the few women to earn a PhD in mathematics in the United States before World War II.<ref name=":0">[[Judy Green (mathematician)|Green, Judy]], and [[Jeanne LaDuke]]. ''Supplementary Material for Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's''. American Mathematical Society, 2009. https://www.ams.org/publications/authors/books/postpub/hmath-34-PioneeringWomen.pdf</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Evelyn Wiggin - The Mathematics Genealogy Project |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=6330 |access-date=2024-06-11 |website=www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu}}</ref>

==Early life==
Evelyn Prescott Wiggin was born March 1, 1900, in [[Stratham, New Hampshire]],<ref name="SunDial19641113">{{cite journal |title=Evelyn W. Casner, R-M Teacher, Dies |journal=Sun Dial |date=13 November 1964 |volume=51 |issue=8 |page=3 |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=SDI19641113.1.3 |access-date=4 April 2025}}</ref> to Margaret Prescott Green and George Herbert Wiggin. Her mother died shortly after giving birth to her second daughter in 1905. She attended the Robinson Seminary public secondary school in [[Exeter, New Hampshire]], and then enrolled in [[Wellesley College]] in 1917 where she was a Durant scholar. She graduated as a mathematics major in 1921 and immediately began teaching mathematics at the [[Massena, New York|Massena]] High School in New York.<ref name=":0" />

On March 28, 1922, Wiggin received a letter from professor [[Roland Richardson|Roland George Dwight Richardson]] at [[Brown University]], who said, "at the suggestion of my good friends, Misses [Helen A.] Merrill and [Clara E.] Smith at Wellesley," invited her to apply for a graduate assistant position in the mathematics department at Brown University. He noted that he usually had "four or five students studying for master's degrees each year, half of whom were women." Wiggin took the position and began work toward her M.A. degree in the autumn of 1922. As Richardson's assistant, she also taught classes of girls who were deficient in algebra and geometry. She completed her master's degree in 1924.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="SunDial19641113" />

For the next three years, Wiggin taught mathematics at [[Hood College]] in [[Frederick, Maryland]], and in 1927, she received another note from Richardson encouraging her to continue graduate work saying, "If you care to take some course for credit in absentia here at Brown, I think it could be arranged. I know you will want to keep on with your studies in some sort of way. Possibly you can go to Chicago some summer." She enrolled at the [[University of Chicago]] that same year.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
In 1929, Wiggin joined the faculty of Randolph-Macon Woman's College (R-MWC) (now [[Randolph College]]) in [[Lynchburg, Virginia]], as an associate professor.<ref name="SunDial19290920">{{cite journal |title=Old and New Faculty Welcomed to R.-M.W.C. |journal=Sun Dial |date=20 September 1929 |volume=16 |issue=1 |page=2 |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=SDI19290920.1.2 |access-date=4 April 2025}}</ref> On March 31, 1931, her Randolph colleague [[Gillie Larew]] wrote to [[Gilbert Ames Bliss]], who had been Larew's own doctoral advisor at the University of Chicago, saying, "I want to thank you again for sending us Miss Wiggin and express the hope that we may keep her for a long, long time. She is everything she should be both as teacher and as a person."<ref name=":0" />

In 1935, Wiggin returned to the University of Chicago for a year and finished her dissertation, titled ''A Boundary Value Problem of the Calculus of Variations'', supervised by Gilbert Ames Bliss and William Thomas Reid.<ref name=":1" /> She was awarded her doctorate in 1936<ref name="SunDial19641113" /> and rejoined Randolph-Macon, where, in 1941, she was promoted to full professor.<ref name="NorthernVirginiaDaily19410611">{{cite journal |title=Professors Appointed in R-M System |journal=Northern Virginia Daily |date=11 June 1941 |volume=59 |issue=139 |page=1 |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=NVD19410611.1.1 |access-date=4 April 2025}}</ref> She remained there until her retirement, though she did take several leaves to teach elsewhere, including at Wellesley College, [[Emory University]] and the University of Chicago.<ref name=":0" />

According to [[Judy Green (mathematician)|Judy Green]], Wiggin belonged to several professional societies.<ref name=":0" />
* [[American Mathematical Society]], elected 1923<ref>{{Cite web |date=1923 |title=THE THIRTIETH SUMMER MEETING OF THE AMERICAN MATHEMATICAL SOCIETY |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1923-29-10/S0002-9904-1923-03790-7/S0002-9904-1923-03790-7.pdf |access-date=2024-06-11 |website=AMS}}</ref>
* [[Mathematical Association of America]]
* [[Graduate Women in Science|Sigma Delta Epsilon]]
* [[American Association of University Women]]
* [[American Association of University Professors]]
* [[Phi Beta Kappa]]

== Personal life ==
On June 20, 1956, at age 56, Evelyn Wiggin married Sidney Casner, a retired lawyer, in Chicago, and took the name Evelyn Wiggin Casner. Sidney Casner died around 1962.<ref name=":0" /> Wiggin died at the University of Virginia Hospital in Charlottesville, Virginia, at the age of 64 on November 5, 1964.<ref name="SunDial19641113" />

== Selected publications ==
* Wiggin, E. P., A boundary value problem of the calculus of variations. In Contributions to the Calculus of Variations, 1933–37, 243-75. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. Published version of PhD dissertation. Reviews: JFM 63.0483.03 (H. Boerner); Zbl 017.36203 (L. M. Graves). Review of volume: Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 44:604-09 (A. Dresden). 1937 
* Wiggin, E., "The value of mathematics in a liberal education". ''Math. Mag.'' 19:418. 1945
